extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of medieval Italian municipal history; historians of medieval Tuscany
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of procedural rules, customary practices, and legal privileges governing the commune of Siena (consular elections, podestà appointment, imperial investiture, inter-city dispute settlement) in the 12th–13th centuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperial privilege forbidding rebuilding of nearby castles
rubrics_metrics.description: Privilege granted to the Sienese that 'neither those counts, nor any other lords, nor their successors, should rebuild any castle, or fortress, within twelve miles of their city.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frederick granted this to prevent neighbouring lords from reestablishing strongholds close to Siena; the rule served as a territorial-security guarantee in favour of the commune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consuls must accept investiture from the emperor/king/legate without expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Elected consuls 'were obliged to accept the investiture of their consulate, without expense, from the king himself, or the emperor, or their successors, if in Italy; if not, from their legate or vicar in Tuscany.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there was no imperial legate in Tuscany, the consuls-elect were obliged to go in a body, or send an ambassador, to demand the investiture of the emperor or king of the Romans; this formalized the tie to imperial authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podestà: foreign magistrate with judicial and military authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The podestà was a foreign nobleman, with 'the judicial authority, in civil and criminal causes,' and 'the government and command of the army in case of war.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Podestà was introduced to separate military matters from civic magistracy and to provide impartial administration; first podestà of Siena (M. Orlando Malaprefa) served for one year according to city order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law (circa 1211): podestà must always be a foreigner
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1211 law declared that 'the podestà should, for the future, always be a foreigner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale given: choosing a foreigner prevented jealousy among local nobles and reduced factional conflict; however the text notes that removing the cause does not always remove effects from entrenched discord.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and composition of consuls (quota distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: At one point it was determined that 'instead of three consuls there should in future be six, observing the same distribution of two thirds noblemen, one third of whom were to be of the Ghibelline faction, and one third popular members.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The city varied the number of consuls ('they went on, varying the number according to the times and the business') to balance ambitions and ease deliberation; changes intended to appease factions but also created practical difficulties assembling magistrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Council discretion in selecting magistrates; opposition to mandatory quotas
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that the council should retain 'the free faculty of making their elections of persons apt for their offices' and against laws imposing 'the necessity of creating one third of them from one faction exclusively.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: mandatory quotas would remove incentive to virtuous behaviour, force councils to select unsuitable candidates, and could produce maladministration; selection should allow choosing those best qualified for times of war or peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for proposing reforms: civil petitioning and council redress
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement that if anyone demanded that anything should be corrected 'he should propose it civilly, without the terror of arms, and, if it should be judged an error or a grievance by the council, there should be no difficulty in obtaining its amendment or redress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the lawful, non-violent channel for redress; the text contrasts it with anti-patterns where armed tumults lead to robberies, conflagrations and universal danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a Tuscan congress/parliament of rectors to settle inter-city disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom to settle disputes 'by a congress or parliament of rectors from all the cities of the league or company of Tuscany; and such deputies... after hearing the parties, and examining witnesses, determined in favour' when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rectors only exercise authority when assembled; their duty was to pursue common utility diligently and to attempt accommodation, and even when failing to avert war they were expected to act for universal benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperial privileges of the commune (elect consuls, coin money, administer justice, exemptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frederick the Second 'renewed and enlarged the privileges of Siena, of administering justice, of paying the gabels or imposts only at the gates of the city, of coining money, and of exemption from all customs and tributes in the country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such privileges strengthened Siena's autonomy but also provoked demands and envy among subject territories and neighbouring cities; they shaped municipal rights and fiscal immunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic custom for assembly locations prior to palace: meeting in parish churches
rubrics_metrics.description: Tuscany's republican cities 'remained long without any palace... they were therefore summoned to meet sometimes in one church, and sometimes in another... until the establishment of the office of the nine, at which time a palace was built.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural custom affected where magistrates assembled and underlined the later institutional development (creation of permanent offices and a palace) as a marker of political maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument against expanding the number of magistrates (governance by multitude is dangerous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Noble argument: 'it has been an infallible observation, that states had been seldom well governed by the multitude... the opinion of the most ignorant and incapable weighs as much as that of the most prudent and experienced.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify restricting magistracies to a limited body and to warn that rashly admitting the multitude to government leads to revolutions and instability; supports selective, competence-based selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement practice: military demonstration and punishment to restore order
rubrics_metrics.description: When the populace continued armed the nobles 'with a great concourse... marched through the city. This procession spread a terror among the seditious, who, from fear, laid down their arms... the government was re-established, and confirmed by the punishment of many of those who had been the heads of this commotion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example illustrating an accepted means of suppressing insurrection: show of force plus punishments to restore civic order; presented as effective though severe remedy.
